work.title: Den døende Jesus. En Passions-Sang. I Fasten opført af det musikalske Selskab

history.p: Due to the political instability caused by the Seven Years' War (1756–63), Scheibe and his family returned to Copenhagen in 1761 having spent twelve years in Sønderborg in the southern part of Denmark. Back in the capital city, Scheibe placed an advertisement in a newspaper announcing that he provided lessons in composition and accompaniment. At the same time he also participated in discussions with, for instance, Heinrich Wilhelm von Gerstenberg on various aspects of rhetoric, declamation and the expression of emotions. For Lent the following year, Scheibe's Passion cantata 'Den døende Jesus' (the dying Jesus) was performed; he chose a text by the 23-year old Morten Hammer. The cantata presents a new direction in the composing of Passion music. Contrary to his previous oratorio, 'Der wundervolle Tod' (SchW B2:313) which is dramatic in character, the present one is lyric. It reveals original developments regarding the orchestral accompaniment in recitatives and is an attempt to employ new theories on the relationship between text and music which Scheibe discusses in his introduction to his 'Der wundervolle Tod' of 1754/1761. The music seeks to express the feelings and emotions of the believers when seeing Jesus on the cross, his suffering and death. The work which consists of two parts clearly relies on Scheibe’s various theoretical writings on the recitative in terms of recitation and declamation for instance that evidently were inspired by his discussions with Gerstenberg. The Passion cantata made a big impression on the audience and was performed several times by The Musical Society. Sometime after Scheibe's death in 1776 the leader of The Royal Orchestra, Claus Nielsen Schall, acquired the manuscript.

annot.p: p. 127: lists Scheibe's Den døende Jesus, Copenhagen 1762, indicating that it is the original score.

'Passions-Concerten, som paa Onsdag opføres i Raadhuus-Strædet, af det Musicalske Selskab, 5te Gang bliver Dansk. Musikken dertil er sadt af den Kongelige Capelmester J. A. Scheibe og Poesien ved M. Hammer. Vi vil her til Prøve anføre et Stykke af den 2den Afdeling [...]'

incipText.p: Hævn Fader! Fader, Gud, Gud, din Søn!
O Salighed! at have Jesum fundet
O Afmagts Røst, jeg af min Jesu Mund maae høre!
O Jesu! Jesu da du saa har elsket mig
O Syn! det Jesu Kors at see!
Ak vee mig! Gud! den haarde Lykke!
O! hvilke Almagts Under! rundt om her udtordne
I Himlens Børn! og nu er jeg forløst, i Brødre!
Ja, dobbelt Raserie sin Salighed forspilde
Flye Verden, flye! jeg min Jesum følge vil
O min Jesu! gid jeg kunde
Triumph! Triumph! Triumph! den Juda Løve vandt

physDesc.watermark: both the Pro Patria emblem with 'GR' and a crown in a circle as well as the countermark 'J HONIG & ZOON' (Heawood:3697, though without '& ZOON') appear in the manuscript which may be found in paper from c. 1724−25); end flyleaf includes WKM below the 'Pro Patria' emblem.
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format; front flyleaf, title page, list of instruments, music (fols. 2r–91r; numbered 1−181), blank page (fol. 91v; p. 182), end flyleaf; in all 46 bifolios. Hand-ruled paper, 16, 19 and 20 staves (8 mm; single rastrum used) in brown and black ink, and music and text in black ink. The score contains some minor autograph changes in black ink, and only a few additions in pencil all of which are recent and probably added during the production of a copy in the 1940s. The eighth movement is the basis of SchW B2:306, 'Duetto & Coro'. Front flyleaf has 'C. Schall' added in ink and final music page (p. 181): 'Soli Deo Gloria!'.

Original half-binding with leather spine and corners, marbled paper; binding is similar to those of SchW B2:430 and B2:439 (Weyses Samling). Title on spine: 'DEN | DØENDE | JESUS | EN | PASSIONS | SANG | A. F | SCHEIBE' in gold lettering and '42' added in black ink. Dutch paper of a fairly dense quality.

physDesc.physMedium: In 8o; title page (sig. [)(1r]; p. [1]), blank page (sig. [)(v]; p. [2]), text (pp. [3]–16); in all 16 pages. A clean copy. No date provided but two added in pencil on title page: '1779 (W).' and '1762 (V.C.R.)', the latter most likely referring to V.C. Ravn (1886).
In limp binding presumably form the early nineteenth century. Paper of a fairly good quality.
